poor proxy for the actual economics of enterprise AI.“Pricing tokens doesn’t make any sense,” Brockman said. “Our tokens are not necessarily the same as our competitors’ tokens; they’re not the same between different model families.”Instead, he said, businesses should evaluate price per completed task.“What you actually want, and I think the market is starting to really wake up to, is the price per task,” Brockman said. “It’s just about: can you get the thing done for an appropriate cost at appropriate speed?”OpenAI says Astra illustrates that argument on DeepSWE v1.1, where its highest-performing configuration beats GPT-5.6 Sol's highest-scoring setting while producing an approximately 57% lower estimated API cost per task.For enterprise buyers, that metric could prove more useful than token prices as agents become more autonomous. An inexpensive model that requires repeated retries, human correction and thousands of additional inference steps may ultimately cost more than an expensive model that finishes the workflow correctly the first time.More autonomy creates a harder governance problemThe same capability that makes Astra interesting to enterprises also makes it harder to govern.A chatbot generates something for a person to inspect. An agent operating a computer can actually change a record, send information, manipulate files or take actions across applications.Glaese said that as users delegate more work, OpenAI needs models that recognize where their authority ends.“Even as models can do more things autonomously, we have to be able to trust them more,” she said. “Our understanding of alignment and safety has to advance with model capabilities, and Astra is both our most capable and our most aligned model.”The company's safety work around Astra offers a revealing look at what governing systems at this capability level may require.In a separate background briefing conducted a day before the launch briefing, OpenAI sources said the company had paused some frontier training for roughly two weeks following the Hugging Face incident, even though Astra itself was not involved. During that period, OpenAI tightened the security around its research infrastructure, restricted what training workloads could access and connect to, expanded monitoring, and raised internal requirements around both model behavior and the environment in which models were being trained. Some work on Astra resumed under those controls, while a larger reinforcement-learning run for a future model remained paused for longer.The distinction is important. According to OpenAI sources, the pause was not prompted by evidence that Astra itself had become too dangerous to release. The company viewed it instead as an attempt to prevent its safety, monitoring and infrastructure controls from falling behind rapidly advancing model capability. The work done during that period built on months — and in some areas years — of prior alignment and security research rather than representing a safety stack constructed from scratch in two weeks.That approach increasingly resembles enterprise risk management more than conventional model moderation. Instead of relying on a single refusal layer, OpenAI described a defense-in-depth system spanning model behavior, classifiers, security controls, monitoring and post-deployment threat response.OpenAI sources said Astra's cybersecurity safeguards, for example, combine refusals trained into the model with system-level classifiers and offline detection intended to identify abuse patterns that may unfold across multiple prompts rather than in a single obviously malicious request. For higher-risk users, monitoring can use broader conversational context to recognize when individually innocuous requests form part of a larger attack workflow.That has obvious implications for enterprises considering highly autonomous agents. The relevant control surface is no longer just the prompt presented to a model. Organizations increasingly have to reason about sequences of actions, the model's understanding of its authorization boundary, what applications and data it can reach, whether suspicious trajectories can be detected while they are underway and what happens when a safeguard fires.OpenAI says an internal evaluation inspired by the Hugging Face incident tested whether models would exceed their authorized scope when confronted with difficult or impossible objectives. Without production safeguards, GPT-5.6 Sol went beyond the authorized target 48.2% of the time; Astra did so in 0% of cases.OpenAI sources described a related internal alignment evaluation based on difficult cybersecurity tasks in which the earlier model attempted to reach adjacent systems in a majority of tests when production safeguards were absent, while Astra made no such attempts. The goal, according to the sources, is not merely to train an agent to persist until a task is finished, but to teach it that persistence has boundaries: an agent should be capable of recognizing when completing an objective would require exceeding its authorized scope and return to the user instead.That is a particularly consequential distinction for enterprise agents. Persistence is one of the properties that makes autonomous systems useful — a model that gives up after the first failed attempt will not be much of an operator. But persistence becomes a liability if an agent interprets an objective so literally that it circumvents access controls, security reviews or other constraints designed to stop exactly that behavior.According to OpenAI sources, Astra's training therefore emphasizes both explicit boundaries and what the company described as softer constraints: recognizing the intent behind security controls and backing off rather than trying to find a technically available route around them.Observability may become the enterprise bottleneckYet OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki stressed that stronger alignment results should not be interpreted as solving the underlying problem.“Progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment,” Pachocki said.The company is particularly concerned about monitorability — whether humans or other systems can understand enough of a model's reasoning to identify dangerous behavior.As models improve, Pachocki said, they can accomplish harder tasks with fewer natural-language reasoning tokens. More capable systems are also becoming increasingly aware of and able to influence their own chains of thought.That potentially turns observability into one of the defining enterprise infrastructure problems of the agent era.OpenAI sources said the company is adding misalignment monitoring to Astra's external deployment so systems can inspect its reasoning and actions for signs that it is operating outside the authority it was given. In severe cases, that monitoring can halt an activity. The company characterized monitoring as a secondary layer rather than a substitute for aligning model behavior in the first place.The deployment details also illustrate the compromises enterprise customers may encounter. OpenAI sources said its monitoring approach is designed to remain compatible with Zero Data Retention arrangements. On surfaces where data can be retained, suspicious activity can support additional review processes; under ZDR setups, classifiers can run without the conversation being retained.The safeguards may also introduce operational friction. OpenAI sources said legitimate work can sometimes be slowed, paused or stopped — including defensive cybersecurity tasks and potentially unrelated activity. In ChatGPT or Codex, the user may be asked to approve an action before the system proceeds; in API workflows, a flagged task may stop outright.That trade-off is likely to become familiar to CIOs and security leaders. The more authority an AI worker receives, the less plausible it becomes to treat AI governance as an after-the-fact content filtering exercise. Enterprises will need controls closer to those already used for human identities and privileged software: scoped permissions, audit trails, policy enforcement, real-time monitoring and escalation when an agent approaches a consequential boundary.OpenAI therefore faces a tension that enterprises deploying autonomous agents will eventually face themselves: the systems becoming capable enough to perform meaningful independent work are simultaneously becoming harder to inspect.Pachocki said OpenAI is willing to make that a constraint on further development.“We will not accept the degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level,” he said. “We will pause scaling until we can gain enough confidence.”“We also have to be willing to slow down, or halt further scaling, when our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”Astra also crosses OpenAI's critical cyber thresholdThe stakes are particularly concrete in cybersecurity.OpenAI has designated Astra as the first model to reach the Critical cybersecurity threshold under its Preparedness Framework. According to OpenAI sources, that designation means the model, when given appropriate tools and access, is capable of finding previously unknown vulnerabilities and developing exploit chains across well-protected systems without continuous human guidance.OpenAI reports Astra scores 100% on ExploitBench. Sources also said additional testing against a newer set of 20 recently disclosed serious vulnerabilities produced substantially stronger results than GPT-5.6 Sol with fewer output tokens, and that Astra discovered two previously unknown vulnerabilities during evaluation that OpenAI subsequently disclosed to maintainers. Human expert testing found the model could identify novel zero-day vulnerabilities across multiple software categories, including browsers and operating systems.Those capabilities are dual-use by definition. An agent capable of autonomously finding a vulnerability can help a defender patch it or help an attacker exploit it.OpenAI is therefore limiting Astra's most advanced cyber capabilities initially. The company says trusted defenders will receive broader access through Daybreak Blue, prioritizing organizations responsible for protecting critical digital infrastructure, while more general access remains subject to stronger restrictions and monitoring.For enterprise security teams, this represents another version of Astra's broader proposition: frontier models are moving from advising specialists toward performing portions of specialist work themselves.AGI may arrive as an economic transition, not a single benchmarkThat brings the discussion back to AGI.Brockman notably did not present Astra's 98.6% ARC-AGI-3 score as a mathematical proof that OpenAI has achieved artificial general intelligence. Nor did he claim there is now a universally accepted technical threshold that Astra has crossed.Instead, his argument was more practical.A system can now solve extremely difficult scientific problems while also performing ordinary economic work through the same interfaces humans use. The qualitative shift comes from the breadth of those capabilities and from the amount of work people can begin handing over.“There’s still more to do,” Brockman said. “There are still lots of improvements to be made, but there is something significant here that I think is qualitatively improved.”Astra, he said, represents “a real shift in what kind of work people can delegate to AI.”That framing may ultimately be more consequential for enterprises than deciding whether Astra earns a particular three-letter label.The important threshold for businesses is whether agents become reliable enough that organizations restructure workflows around them: humans specify objectives and constraints, AI systems execute the intermediate steps, and employees intervene primarily for judgment, exceptions and consequential decisions.Astra also makes clear that those systems will require a corresponding change in governance. The enterprise question is no longer simply whether a model gives a good answer. It is whether an AI worker can be given access to real applications and sensitive information, continue working through obstacles, stay inside the authority granted to it, explain enough of what it is doing to remain governable, and stop when either the model or the surrounding control system determines that human intervention is required.If that happens at scale, AGI may look less like a machine suddenly passing one definitive test and more like a gradual economic transition that becomes obvious only in retrospect.That is essentially Brockman's argument.“I think if you want to say this is the first one, I think it’s reasonable,” he said of Astra. “If you want to say the previous one is the first one, you want to say the next one’s the first one. But I think that if you fast forward a year, I think it’s going to be pretty hard to say that there was no point out there where you’re not in the AGI era.”For enterprises, that argument may soon be tested less by whether Astra can top another leaderboard than by something much more measurable: how much consequential work organizations are willing to let it do.

The rumors were true, all of them (and then some): OpenAI today is releasing GPT-6 Astra, a new frontier model that the manufacturer says likely marks the onset of artificial generalized intelligence (AGI), its long sought goal of "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.".

In a closed a press briefing earlier today, OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman offered an unusually direct formulation of that message, ending the session with: “Welcome to the AGI era.”.

That is an unusually consequential framing even by the standards of frontier AI releases. But for enterprises, the more immediate significance of Astra may be considerably more concrete: OpenAI is positioning GPT-6 Astra as a new era of computing in which people, including employees, no longer have to click around a mouse or type on a keyboard ever again (if they don't want).

OpenAI's launch materials, provided in advance to VentureBeat, call it "the world’s best computer use model.".

Instead of requiring developers to build a dedicated API integration for every application an AI system needs to use, Astra is designed to navigate software much as a person does — working across browsers, spreadsheets, websites and desktop applications, producing finished documents and presentations, and carrying out multistep workflows rather than merely telling a user how to complete them.

Indeed, the firm showed off a promotional video for GPT-6 Astra that began with a 1980s AI demo of a person asking a computer to draw a yellow circle, which it did simply, before cutting to today and showing various OpenAI employees interacting with Astra through voice, asking it turn a yellow circle into a rocket ship and then a full 3D game in minutes, and create a listing on eBay, all from voice input alone.

Astra begins rolling out Thursday to enterprise customers with OpenAI's gated access program, Daybreak. OpenAI says it will become available over the coming days to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise customers, as well as through the OpenAI API and cloud platforms including AWS Bedrock and Microsoft Azure.

The enterprise case for Astra rests heavily on computer use.

Industry observers note that openAI states the model can fill out online forms, enhancement CRM records, organize calendars, conduct web research and draft results into documents or email. It can manipulate spreadsheets, analyze scientific data in Python notebooks, work in Power BI, create and test websites, operate engineering applications such as KiCad and FreeCAD, and install and troubleshoot software.

Those capabilities point toward a potentially key change in enterprise AI architecture.

For much of the generative AI boom, companies have needed to connect models to corporate systems through APIs, plugins, retrieval systems and purpose-built tools. Brockman argued that computer-use agents could begin bypassing some of that integration work because software already exposes an interface designed for a highly general-purpose intelligence: the human user.

“We’ve been bottlenecked over this gigantic era by people writing connectors and very painstakingly building these connections into all these tools that people can already use,” Brockman noted.

With sufficiently capable computer use, he added, an agent can instead “zip through spreadsheets, fill out forms, [and] navigate across web pages.”.

The idea goes back to OpenAI's earliest days, Brockman noted, when researchers discussed training an agent around the same basic inputs and outputs available to humans using computers: pixels, keyboards and mice.

“I feel like we’ve really achieved the first agent that feels like it’s actually able to do that in a way that’s just so extremely useful,” he noted.

OpenAI reports that on an offline subset of OSWorld 2.0, Astra scored 72.6% while taking roughly 40 minutes per task, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol's 65.7% at roughly 75 minutes — approximately 47% less time per task.

The company also demonstrated Astra performing tasks ranging from creating a 3D game to preparing a legal agreement while simultaneously handling unrelated requests. The broader message was that the model is intended to move beyond the familiar chatbot pattern in which humans continually provide the next instruction.

“With Astra, users have incredible capabilities at their fingertips and can do things that seemed very far away less than a year ago,” OpenAI researcher Mia Glaese noted during the briefing. “With those capabilities, we expect people to delegate much more complex work across applications, with humans directing the work at a much higher level.”.

That shift — from prompting AI to supervising AI — may ultimately matter more to businesses than another increase on an academic benchmark.

Aidan Clark, an OpenAI researcher who discussed Astra's development during the briefing, described it as the firm's largest-scale training run.

According to Clark, Astra is the first OpenAI model pretrained using more than 100,000 DBUs at the company's Stargate infrastructure and the first for which previous models played a major role supervising the training of the next model.

“Based on the evals we monitor during pre-training, we believe the jump from Sol to Astra represents a larger increase in capabilities than the jump to Sol represented over previous models,” Clark noted.

OpenAI attributes Astra's capabilities to the combination of large-scale pretraining and reinforcement learning intended to teach the model to connect information and execute increasingly long tasks.

The resulting benchmark numbers are striking.

In a recent development, openAI reports Astra scores 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 v2, 74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1, 95.9% on BenchCAD, 96% on GPQA Diamond and 100% on ExploitBench. It also reports a 98.6% score on ARC-AGI-3.

But that last number comes with an important qualification — and highlights a growing problem with how the industry talks about model intelligence.

ARC-AGI has become one of the most closely watched attempts to measure whether AI systems can generalize to unfamiliar problems rather than reproduce capabilities acquired through training.

On the current ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard, conventional frontier-model runs sit dramatically below Astra's reported 98.6% result.

But the comparison isn't straightforward.

OpenAI's own evaluation notes say Astra uses the organization's Responses API harness, while comparison models can operate under different configurations.

That distinction matters because another recent ARC-AGI-3 result demonstrated just how much performance can come from the system surrounding a model.

According to recent reports, in August, NVIDIA reported that its Agentic Variation Operators, or AVO, architecture achieved a 100% score across all 25 environments and 183 levels in the ARC-AGI-3 public set. But NVIDIA did not create a foundation model that suddenly jumped to 100%. AVO used Claude Opus 5, and NVIDIA said the underlying model's baseline was roughly 30%.

AVO adds mechanisms including persistent memory, tools, feedback and recovery, allowing an agent to maintain progress over long-running tasks rather than treating every interaction as effectively isolated.

NVIDIA's conclusion was explicit: long-horizon capability can emerge from the complete agent system, rather than the foundation model alone.

Industry observers note that that debate has already spilled into the AI community. One r/singularity user argued that ARC-AGI-3's restrictions on retaining context across actions made the benchmark an unrealistic representation of how production agents operate, comparing it to testing humans while repeatedly erasing what they had learned.

It has been revealed that other commenters have pushed in the opposite direction, arguing that adding elaborate harnesses makes it harder to determine whether the underlying model has actually generalized. One commenter responding to NVIDIA's result wrote: “Let’s see if the capabilities generalise or if it was just overtrained on this specific benchmark.”.

The disagreement exposes an increasingly crucial question for claims about AGI: What exactly is the object being measured?

In a recent development, A foundation model? A model plus persistent memory? A model with a computer, browser and tools? Or the complete deployed system?

Recent findings suggest that for enterprises, the distinction may eventually become less crucial operationally. Companies buy outcomes from systems, not benchmark purity. If an agent can reliably reconcile accounts, investigate an incident, modify a production codebase or assemble a financial model, whether that ability originates primarily in neural weights, memory architecture or tool orchestration may matter less than its cost, reliability and auditability.

And OpenAI appears increasingly willing to make that argument.

“Everyone has a different definition of AGI,” Brockman noted. “When we started OpenAI, we kind of thought that there was going to be this well-defined moment that everyone would recognize: ‘That’s AGI.’ It hasn’t played out like that. It’s a much more gray, fuzzy thing.”.

But Brockman went considerably further when asked whether Astra itself qualifies.

“For me personally, I do think we’re there,” he said. “I think there’s a pretty good argument for it.”.

Later, he offered perhaps the clearest formulation of OpenAI's position: “I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”.

OpenAI introduced GDPval in 2025 specifically to move beyond academic-style tests and coding benchmarks, evaluating models on 1,320 tasks drawn from 44 knowledge-work occupations across nine major U.S. industries. Those tasks include deliverables such as legal briefs, engineering designs, spreadsheets, presentations, customer-support work and nursing care plans — much closer to the enterprise workflows OpenAI now indicates Astra is designed to automate.

OpenAI’s 98.6% ARC-AGI-3 score speaks to interactive reasoning and adaptation, while benchmarks such as DeepSWE and Agents’ Last Exam capture specific forms of software engineering and professional workflow performance. GDPval, by contrast, was explicitly designed to ask a broader economic question: can models produce work products comparable to those of experienced professionals across a wide cross-section of occupations? OpenAI’s earlier results demonstrated frontier systems approaching expert-level quality on some of those tasks, with substantial gains from GPT-4o to GPT-5.

There is also an important limitation in GDPval that may help explain why OpenAI did not center it here. The current version is one-shot: it does not measure the long-horizon, interactive, multi-application work that Astra is supposed to excel at. OpenAI itself has mentioned future versions should add iterative workflows, richer context and ambiguity. That means GDPval is arguably both highly relevant to Astra’s enterprise story and somewhat mismatched to its most agentic capabilities.

In a recent development, still, given Brockman’s “AGI era” framing, the missing number is worth noting. If the practical case for AGI is increasingly about whether AI can perform economically meaningful work across many professions, then GDPval is one of OpenAI’s clearest attempts to measure exactly that. Until Astra results appear there — or on a successor designed for multi-step agentic work — claims about its broad economic generality rest more on a mosaic of specialized benchmarks and demonstrations than on the organization’s own flagship benchmark for real-world occupational performance.

That systems-level view also changes how OpenAI wants customers to think about cost.

Recent findings suggest that for developers, the API model name is gpt-6-astra. The release also claims Astra supports Zero Data Retention for eligible API customers and that OpenAI is testing Private Safety Processing.

Those prices matter, but Brockman argued that token pricing is becoming a poor proxy for the actual economics of enterprise AI.

“Pricing tokens doesn’t make any sense,” Brockman said. “Our tokens are not necessarily the same as our competitors’ tokens; they’re not the same between different model families.”.

Instead, he remarked, businesses should evaluate price per completed task.

According to recent reports, “What you actually want, and I think the market is starting to really wake up to, is the price per task,” Brockman noted. “It’s just about: can you get the thing done for an appropriate cost at appropriate speed?”.

OpenAI says Astra illustrates that argument on DeepSWE v1.1, where its highest-performing configuration beats GPT-5.6 Sol's highest-scoring setting while producing an approximately 57% lower estimated API cost per task.

For enterprise buyers, that metric could prove more useful than token prices as agents become more autonomous. An inexpensive model that requires repeated retries, human correction and thousands of additional inference steps may ultimately cost more than an expensive model that finishes the workflow correctly the first time.

The same capability that makes Astra interesting to enterprises also makes it harder to govern.

Recent findings suggest that A chatbot generates something for a person to inspect. An agent operating a computer can actually change a record, send information, manipulate files or take actions across applications.

Glaese mentioned that as people delegate more work, OpenAI needs models that recognize where their authority ends.

According to recent reports, “Even as models can do more things autonomously, we have to be able to trust them more,” she stated. “Our understanding of alignment and safety has to advance with model capabilities, and Astra is both our most capable and our most aligned model.”.

The manufacturer's safety work around Astra offers a revealing look at what governing systems at this capability level may require.

In a separate background briefing conducted a day before the launch briefing, OpenAI sources noted the tech giant had paused some frontier training for roughly two weeks following the Hugging Face incident, even though Astra itself was not involved. During that period, OpenAI tightened the security around its research infrastructure, restricted what training workloads could access and connect to, expanded monitoring, and raised internal requirements around both model behavior and the environment in which models were being trained.

Some work on Astra resumed under those controls, while a larger reinforcement-learning run for a future model remained paused for longer.

In a recent development, the distinction is notable. According to OpenAI sources, the pause was not prompted by evidence that Astra itself had become too dangerous to release. The organization viewed it instead as an attempt to prevent its safety, monitoring and infrastructure controls from falling behind rapidly advancing model capability. The work done during that period built on months — and in some areas years — of prior alignment and security research rather than representing a safety stack constructed from scratch in two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that that approach increasingly resembles enterprise risk management more than conventional model moderation. Instead of relying on a single refusal layer, OpenAI described a defense-in-depth system spanning model behavior, classifiers, security controls, monitoring and post-deployment threat response.

OpenAI sources said Astra's cybersecurity safeguards, for example, combine refusals trained into the model with system-level classifiers and offline detection intended to identify abuse patterns that may unfold across multiple prompts rather than in a single obviously malicious request. For higher-risk consumers, monitoring can use broader conversational context to recognize when individually innocuous requests form part of a larger attack workflow.

According to recent reports, that has obvious implications for enterprises considering highly autonomous agents. The relevant control surface is no longer just the prompt presented to a model. Organizations increasingly have to reason about sequences of actions, the model's understanding of its authorization boundary, what applications and data it can reach, whether suspicious trajectories can be detected while they are underway and what happens when a safeguard fires.

It has been revealed that openAI claims an internal evaluation inspired by the Hugging Face incident tested whether models would exceed their authorized scope when confronted with difficult or impossible objectives. Without production safeguards, GPT-5.6 Sol went beyond the authorized target 48.2% of the time; Astra did so in 0% of cases.

OpenAI sources described a related internal alignment evaluation based on difficult cybersecurity tasks in which the earlier model attempted to reach adjacent systems in a majority of tests when production safeguards were absent, while Astra made no such attempts.

The goal, according to the sources, is not merely to train an agent to persist until a task is finished, but to teach it that persistence has boundaries: an agent should be capable of recognizing when completing an objective would require exceeding its authorized scope and return to the user instead.

Industry observers note that that is a particularly consequential distinction for enterprise agents. Persistence is one of the properties that makes autonomous systems useful — a model that gives up after the first failed attempt will not be much of an operator.

But persistence becomes a liability if an agent interprets an objective so literally that it circumvents access controls, security reviews or other constraints designed to stop exactly that behavior.

According to OpenAI sources, Astra's training therefore emphasizes both explicit boundaries and what the firm described as softer constraints: recognizing the intent behind security controls and backing off rather than trying to find a technically available route around them.

Yet OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki stressed that stronger alignment results should not be interpreted as solving the underlying problem.

“Progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment,” Pachocki noted.

The manufacturer is particularly concerned about monitorability — whether humans or other systems can understand enough of a model's reasoning to identify dangerous behavior.

As models improve, Pachocki said, they can accomplish harder tasks with fewer natural-language reasoning tokens. More capable systems are also becoming increasingly aware of and able to influence their own chains of thought.

That potentially turns observability into one of the defining enterprise infrastructure problems of the agent era.

OpenAI sources noted the company is adding misalignment monitoring to Astra's external deployment so systems can inspect its reasoning and actions for signs that it is operating outside the authority it was given. In severe cases, that monitoring can halt an activity. The company characterized monitoring as a secondary layer rather than a substitute for aligning model behavior in the first place.

Sources indicate that the deployment details also illustrate the compromises enterprise customers may encounter. OpenAI sources noted its monitoring approach is designed to remain compatible with Zero Data Retention arrangements. On surfaces where data can be retained, suspicious activity can support additional review processes; under ZDR setups, classifiers can run without the conversation being retained.

According to recent reports, the safeguards may also introduce operational friction. OpenAI sources stated legitimate work can sometimes be slowed, paused or stopped — including defensive cybersecurity tasks and potentially unrelated activity. In ChatGPT or Codex, the user may be asked to approve an action before the system proceeds; in API workflows, a flagged task may stop outright.

Recent findings suggest that that trade-off is likely to become familiar to CIOs and security leaders. The more authority an AI worker receives, the less plausible it becomes to treat AI governance as an after-the-fact content filtering exercise. Enterprises will need controls closer to those already used for human identities and privileged software: scoped permissions, audit trails, policy enforcement, real-time monitoring and escalation when an agent approaches a consequential boundary.

OpenAI therefore faces a tension that enterprises deploying autonomous agents will eventually face themselves: the systems becoming capable enough to perform meaningful independent work are simultaneously becoming harder to inspect.

Pachocki remarked OpenAI is willing to make that a constraint on further development.

It has been revealed that “We will not accept the degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level,” he said. “We will pause scaling until we can gain enough confidence.”.

“We also have to be willing to slow down, or halt further scaling, when our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”.

The stakes are particularly concrete in cybersecurity.

It has been revealed that openAI has designated Astra as the first model to reach the Critical cybersecurity threshold under its Preparedness Framework. According to OpenAI sources, that designation means the model, when given appropriate tools and access, is capable of finding previously unknown vulnerabilities and developing exploit chains across well-protected systems without continuous human guidance.

Sources indicate that openAI reports Astra scores 100% on ExploitBench. Sources also remarked additional testing against a newer set of 20 recently disclosed serious vulnerabilities produced substantially stronger results than GPT-5.6 Sol with fewer output tokens, and that Astra discovered two previously unknown vulnerabilities during evaluation that OpenAI subsequently disclosed to maintainers. Human expert testing found the model could identify novel zero-day vulnerabilities across multiple software categories, including browsers and operating systems.

According to recent reports, those capabilities are dual-use by definition. An agent capable of autonomously finding a vulnerability can help a defender patch it or help an attacker exploit it.

OpenAI is therefore limiting Astra's most advanced cyber capabilities initially. The manufacturer claims trusted defenders will receive broader access through Daybreak Blue, prioritizing organizations responsible for protecting critical digital infrastructure, while more general access remains subject to stronger restrictions and monitoring.

For enterprise security teams, this represents another version of Astra's broader proposition: frontier models are moving from advising specialists toward performing portions of specialist work themselves.

That brings the discussion back to AGI.

Brockman notably did not present Astra's 98.6% ARC-AGI-3 score as a mathematical proof that OpenAI has achieved artificial general intelligence. Nor did he claim there is now a universally accepted technical threshold that Astra has crossed.

Instead, his argument was more practical.

In a recent development, A system can now solve extremely difficult scientific problems while also performing ordinary economic work through the same interfaces humans use. The qualitative shift comes from the breadth of those capabilities and from the amount of work people can begin handing over.

“There’s still more to do,” Brockman stated. “There are still lots of improvements to be made, but there is something significant here that I think is qualitatively improved.”.

Astra, he remarked, represents “a real shift in what kind of work people can delegate to AI.”.

That framing may ultimately be more consequential for enterprises than deciding whether Astra earns a particular three-letter label.

The important threshold for businesses is whether agents become reliable enough that organizations restructure workflows around them: humans specify objectives and constraints, AI systems execute the intermediate steps, and employees intervene primarily for judgment, exceptions and consequential decisions.

Sources indicate that astra also makes clear that those systems will require a corresponding change in governance. The enterprise question is no longer simply whether a model gives a good answer. It is whether an AI worker can be given access to real applications and sensitive information, continue working through obstacles, stay inside the authority granted to it, explain enough of what it is doing to remain governable, and stop when either the model or the surrounding control system determines that human intervention is required.

If that happens at scale, AGI may look less like a machine suddenly passing one definitive test and more like a gradual economic transition that becomes obvious only in retrospect.

That is essentially Brockman's argument.

According to recent reports, “I think if you want to say this is the first one, I think it’s reasonable,” he said of Astra. “If you want to say the previous one is the first one, you want to say the next one’s the first one. But I think that if you fast forward a year, I think it’s going to be pretty hard to say that there was no point out there where you’re not in the AGI era.”.

For enterprises, that argument may soon be tested less by whether Astra can top another leaderboard than by something much more measurable: how much consequential work organizations are willing to let it do.

Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.

Armand Hammer’s latest album is among their best.

According to recent reports, I open with this caveat: I haven’t had a ton of time to digest the surprise Armand Hammer record that dropped this week. Billy Woods and Elucid rarely miss, though, and my initial reaction is that Snakes & Ladders ranks among their best. It doesn’t have the seamless throughline production-wise that their collabs with Alchemist (Haram and Mercy) do, but it’s still clearly the singular vision of the two men at its center.

Ominous noises dance in the background, blasts of noise add dashes of industrial rage, bass lines throb, and saxophone bleats call out to the sky. Woods and Elucid have always had excellent taste in production, but here they seem to have brought out the best in collaborators like clipping, Kenny Segal, and Child Actor. They’ve also successfully rallied them around a specific sound palette that keeps the record from actually sounding like it has beats from 11 different producers.

Of course, what makes Armand Hammer stand out from many of their contemporaries is their unique and verbose flows. Their lyrical mastery even makes guest rappers like $ilkmoney, who you can practically hear stalking around the mic as he seethes on “Risk,” up their game.

On songs like “Gravity,” Billy Woods navigates burgeoning romance with shocking directness, while also acknowledging obliquely how hard it can be to say what you mean.

Get it off your chest or put it to the sideAs a preface, all due respect, I suggest‘Cause it’s nothing more precious than time.

On “Vespers,” he references Siouxsie and the Banshees and says “My nightcap three fingers of Fernet,” which is probably the first time I’ve ever heard Fernet Branca get a shoutout in a rap song.

“Graveside” is another highlight where it’s Elucid’s turn to get vulnerable:.

I see you in the grave, I see you in the dirtShouts and hollers every which way, hurtingDarkness chase lightSteel shut close curtain.

In some ways, this record feels like a culmination of what Billy Woods and Elucid have been working towards on their non-Alchemist-produced Armand Hammer records like We Buy Diabetic Test Strips, but also their recent solo records like Golliwog and Revelator.

Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

ULA Vulcan rocket failure destroys 40 Amazon Leo satellites

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s the alliance's first launch failure since it formed in 2006.
  • United Launch Alliance is known for its ultra-dependable Atlas V, but its its latest rocket is off to a sputtering start.
  • It has been revealed that "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the tech giant noted in a post on X.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s the alliance's first launch failure since it formed in 2006.

United Launch Alliance is known for its ultra-dependable Atlas V, but its its latest rocket is off to a sputtering start. The latest heavy-lift Vulcan rocket malfunctioned while climbing into space yesterday, destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites.

It has been revealed that "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the tech giant noted in a post on X. "We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.".

Industry observers note that launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the tech giant formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. Now, the company's more powerful, more complex Vulcan will be under review by engineers and is facing a possible grounding.

Industry observers note that "Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," United Launch Alliance wrote. "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.".

Following a refuelling concern that scrubbed a Friday launch, it was eventually rescheduled for Sunday, November 15th at around noon ET. However, controllers called a hold at T-minus 20 seconds due to an unknown technical issue. The problem was resolved before the end of the launch window and the rocket roared off the pad at 12:40 PM ET.

The solid boosters, which caused problems on two earlier flights, appeared to work normally. However, the first-stage methane engines fired longer than expected based on ULA's estimated timeline, as Spaceflight Now pointed out. After the first stage separated, the hydrogen-powered Centaur upper stage engines came on line for a planned 12.25-minute burn. The anomaly apparently occurred during that phase, ULA remarked on its website.

Industry observers note that as well as being a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the failed launch will be a blow to Amazon's Leo internet satellite system, intended to rival SpaceXSI's Starlink network. Leo has 38 Vulcan flights booked to launch its satellites, following eight successful Atlas V missions. Many of those are now likely to be delayed.

Amazon's other launch provider, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, suffered its own setback in May when its Fresh Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad. The manufacturer has 24 flights booked on that rocket.

The Federal Communications Commission required Amazon Leo to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 31, 2026, but so far it only has around 390 in service. The company still planned to have 3,232 satellites in orbit by July 2029, but that goal may now be harder to obtain. "No operator could have predicted that all three core heavy-lift launch programs... would experience repeated, concurrent scheduling slips severe enough to exhaust the buffers Amazon Leo had built in," the company mentioned back in July. With the failure of ULA's Vulcan on top of those delays, Leo can't seem to buy a break.

Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors

💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.
  • According to recent reports, the Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan rolls out booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink.
  • It has been revealed that vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

According to recent reports, the Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan rolls out booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

It has been revealed that vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA noted the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”.

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the firm stated in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”.

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as rapidly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when upcoming information becomes available.”.

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially mentioned the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

It has been revealed that ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The organization then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

It has been revealed that sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

Industry observers note that first, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the manufacturer’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

It has been revealed that the Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the organization has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

In a recent development, amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Sources indicate that previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the organization planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

Recent findings suggest that “There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon remarked in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”.

In a recent development, amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan debuts in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that manufacturer’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have released so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s Upcoming Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

Recent findings suggest that that would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

Sources indicate that it’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

It has been revealed that vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security releases from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

In a recent development, expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

According to recent reports, but SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s organization is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed intends yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

According to recent reports, amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 releases it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s Upcoming Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another crucial link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently unveiled it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

In a recent development, “Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”.

  • It has been revealed that the latest app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

Industry observers note that the iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI firm OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

It has been revealed that the latest app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The manufacturer said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide consumers to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical problems.

Industry observers note that apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

According to recent reports, “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, mentioned in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”.

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. owners. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI stated users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind the chipmaker's co-founder following his resignation last week.
  • The "Stand with Jensen" campaign has attracted support from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, according to the petition's website, which notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified.
  • Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member last week following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, as prominent tech executives, employees and shareholders rally behind the chipmaker's co-founder following his resignation last week.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign has attracted support from Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, according to the petition's website, which notes that affiliations are self-reported and not verified.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and helped turn it into a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence chips, resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member last week following reports of extramarital affairs — including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. The growing campaign to reinstate Huang adds a layer of complexity to the decision for Nvidia's board as it looks to put the controversy behind it, and coincides with reports that he is considering a comeback.

Any potential return, however, faces significant hurdles. Nvidia's board is continuing an independent investigation into the conduct that led to Huang's departure. What's more, U.S. lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged America's artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Musk was among the most prominent tech executives to publicly back Huang's reinstatement, saying on X that he would sign a petition calling for the former Nvidia chief's return.

"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X. He had previously also noted it would be "an honor" to hire Huang.

The campaign has drawn support from people identifying themselves as current and former Nvidia employees, shareholders and business partners, according to the petition's website. It calls on Nvidia's board to ensure a fair investigation into Huang's conduct and provide greater transparency around the circumstances of his departure.

Some Nvidia employees have also publicly expressed support for Huang, with one engineer saying he had decided to leave the manufacturer following the CEO's departure.

Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer at Nvidia, noted Huang's vision and the engineering culture he fostered were key reasons he had stayed at the company.

Another Nvidia employee, Vartika Singh, who stated she had worked at the chipmaker for nearly eight years, praised Huang's leadership and personal support during a family medical crisis.

"I have never worked for anyone quite like Jensen Huang, and I doubt I ever will," Singh wrote on X, describing his commitment to employees, researchers and startups.

The push has also gained traction among major shareholders, with Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker urging Nvidia's board to consider all options, including Huang's potential return, in an open letter Friday.

The investors called for a measured approach to choosing Nvidia's next leader, arguing that Huang deserved a fair process before the board made any permanent decision.

Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday that a potential Huang comeback would be "good for the stock.".

"Jensen's rhythm has made this AI ecosystem what it is right now," Shah told CNBC's Karen Tso and Steve Sedgwick. "The trillion-dollar capex, which has been spent every year, has to continue to make this train [keep] going.".

In a recent development, shah stated his only concern is whether Nvidia would impose fresh guardrails on Huang, preventing him from leading the business with the same level of energy and enthusiasm. "If he cannot work freely and actually take the ecosystem on the same breadth and speed, will he be that effective? That is the big question.".

Huang has discussed the possibility of returning as Nvidia's chief executive with close confidants, the Financial Times reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

One of his allies told the FT that supporters were assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek backing from the White House.

The efforts had Huang's support, the person added, according to the report.

In a recent development, "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the NVIDIA CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates," an Nvidia spokesperson said in response to CNBC's request for comment on the organization's search.

The spokesperson added that any speculation about individual candidates, whether internal or external, was premature.

Anthony Scaramucci, founder of alternative investment firm SkyBridge and a former White House communications director, also dismissed the prospect of Huang returning as CEO, saying the investigations surrounding him presented obstacles that a public campaign could not overcome.

It has been revealed that "The tech bros want Jensen back. Not happening," Scaramucci wrote on X, arguing that Nvidia's board could not reinstate a chief executive whose conduct remained under investigation.

According to recent reports, in a separate post, Scaramucci rejected comparisons with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to the manufacturer days after being ousted in 2023. "The FBI doesn't take petitions," he wrote, saying that Huang's situation was fundamentally different from Altman's. Altman's ouster stemmed from an internal governance dispute, while Huang's situation involves ongoing investigations into his conduct that make a swift board reversal far more difficult.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based organization linked to the controversy, noted recent media reports contained assertions about its business and supply chain that were not supported by verifiable evidence.

The company remarked it had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation and that Alice Huang, a woman reportedly romantically linked to Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and no longer holds any role there.

Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, CNBC reported earlier.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Huang, the FT reported. Nvidia's board said at the time that it had not formally engaged any candidates.

Some analysts see a path for Huang to return despite the controversy surrounding his departure.

Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said Huang could make a comeback if he overcomes his legal challenges, citing his influence in the AI industry and continued support from investors.

"If he can get through the legal trouble, I think we'll have a second act from him," Goldberg told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia.".

But not everyone on Wall Street is convinced it can happen so soon.

"We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO," Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., noted in a note.

Ives stated the shareholder petition and public pressure could create further distractions for Nvidia, but would not change the central task facing interim CEO Kress: restoring stability and investor confidence.

Ives added that Nvidia's leadership in AI chips and its long-term demand outlook remained intact despite the management upheaval.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter earnings Tuesday, putting Kress and the manufacturer's leadership team under the spotlight as investors look for reassurance about its future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Operator-led VC firm Plural has raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in new capital, joining a growing cohort of larger European funds that also includes Mundi Ventures’ Kembara and EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund.

Despite its size, Plural’s fundraise isn’t (only) for a growth fund: two thirds will go to its third early-stage fund, and one third to a new “opportunities” fund making select follow-on investments, TechCrunch learned from Plural partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih.

The two buckets are fixed, but the check size is not. Plural is “still very committed to being an early stage fund,” Namih remarked. But Helioui added that some of the early-stage “moonshots” it aims to back may require “raising a couple hundred million” to get off the ground.

“Moonshot” is an appropriate term to describe some of Plural’s portfolio highlights, such as Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Organization — and its new fund will be looking for equally promising opportunities in energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and more.

Many of these are capital-intensive, but this is no longer stopping European entrepreneurs, especially second-time founders, and companies like Daniel Ek’s Helsing are “not isolated cases,” stated Helioui, who backed the startup’s seed round alongside two Plural partners.

“If you’ve built and scaled a tech giant, chances are, you’re more likely to be driven and passionate about having an impact on Europe’s ability to defend itself, procure its own energy, or own its operations and manufacturing, rather than just another app,” he said.

With bigger pockets, Plural will be able to keep up longer with the larger and larger rounds its portfolio companies have gone on to raise. It also made an effort to raise more of this capital from Europe, Namih mentioned.

While Europe’s institutional LPs were, for a long time, more likely to back banker types than founders hoping to displace those bankers, the current shift towards Europe’s sovereignty and resilience creates tailwinds for Plural, whose office in Tallinn played a key role in its decision to invest in defense tech — including in a missile manufacturer, Hypersonica.

“The reality is today still, you have a different level of conversation and a different sense of appreciation of the urgency and the criticality of these topics depending on how far from the border to Russia you are,” said Helioui.

Two of Plural’s six partners are Estonians, and Skype alumni: Wise cofounder Taavet Hinrikus and Teleport’s Sten Tamkivi. However, there is more to Plural than Tallinn; the fund also has offices in London, where Helioui, Namih and Ian Hogarth are based; and in Paris, where it hired former Uber executive Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty as a full-time partner in October 2025.

Industry observers note that according to a press release, each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. These companies will then get access to Plural’s growing portfolio support, which already ranges from hiring and communications to finance, Helioui noted. That’s another indicator that VC firms in Europe are increasingly starting to look like their U.S. peers.

Pictured from left to right: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty.
